items.followUp: What is the role of the S phase in the cell cycle?

rubric.why: Identifies the general changes in G2.
rubric.description: Continued cell growth and preparation for cell division.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the cell continues to grow or prepares for mitosis in G2.

rubric.why: Names materials produced for the upcoming division.
rubric.description: Synthesis of proteins and organelles needed for division.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the synthesis of proteins and/or organelles needed for cell division.

modelAnswer: During G2, the cell continues to grow and prepares for mitosis.
It synthesizes proteins and organelles needed for cell division.

items.followUp: State two ways in which mitosis helps an organism.

rubric.why: Connects mitosis with an increase in cell number and growth.
rubric.description: Mitosis increases the number of cells, allowing the organism to grow.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that mitosis increases cell number and supports growth.

rubric.why: Recognizes mitosis's role in tissue maintenance or development.
rubric.description: Mitosis replaces or repairs cells and supports development from the zygote.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either cell replacement/repair or development from the zygote.

modelAnswer: Mitosis produces more cells, increasing cell number and enabling growth.
It replaces or repairs damaged and worn-out cells and helps in the development of an organism from the zygote.

items.followUp: At what stage of meiosis does crossing over occur, and what is its result?

rubric.why: Defines crossing over by identifying the chromatids and chromosomes involved.
rubric.description: Exchange of corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct exchange and its location in prophase I.

rubric.why: Assesses whether the answer includes a meaningful labeled representation of the exchange.
rubric.description: Diagram showing an exchange between two non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a diagram that shows the exchange and identifies the chromatids or homologous chromosomes.

modelAnswer: Crossing over is the exchange of corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.
Diagram (letters represent chromosome segments):
Before:  Chromatid 1: A—B—C—D
Chromatid 2: a—b—c—d
After:    Chromatid 1: A—B—c—d
Chromatid 2: a—b—C—D
The exchanged segments produce new combinations of genetic material.

items.followUp: Name the three main components of an ATP molecule.

rubric.why: Checks identification of ATP's molecular components.
rubric.description: ATP consists of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming all three components.

rubric.why: Assesses the structural drawing and its key labels.
rubric.description: A labeled structure showing adenosine linked to three phosphate groups, with high-energy bonds between phosphate groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct labeled structure showing the three linked phosphate groups.

modelAnswer: ATP consists of adenine, ribose sugar and three phosphate groups.
Molecular structure: Adenine—Ribose—P~P~P
The ~ bonds between the phosphate groups are high-energy bonds.

items.followUp: What is the difference between a linear and a cyclic metabolic pathway?

rubric.why: Checks that a metabolic pathway is described as a sequence of reactions.
rubric.description: A metabolic pathway is a series or sequence of chemical reactions occurring in a cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a pathway as a series or sequence of reactions in the cell.

rubric.why: Checks the enzyme control and connection between successive reactions.
rubric.description: The reactions are enzyme-controlled, and the product of one reaction can become the substrate for the next.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining enzyme control or the product-to-substrate link between reactions.

modelAnswer: A metabolic pathway is a series of chemical reactions that occur in a cell.
Each reaction is controlled by an enzyme, and the product of one reaction may become the substrate for the next reaction.

items.followUp: How does the shape of an enzyme's active site help it catalyse a reaction?

rubric.why: Identifies the active site and its role in binding the substrate.
rubric.description: The active site is the specific region of an enzyme where the substrate binds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as the enzyme region where the substrate binds.

rubric.why: Explains the specific fit between substrate and active site.
rubric.description: The active site's shape is complementary to the substrate, allowing an enzyme-substrate complex to form.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the complementary fit or formation of the enzyme-substrate complex.

modelAnswer: The active site is the specific region of an enzyme to which its substrate binds.
Its shape is complementary to the substrate, so an enzyme-substrate complex can form.

items.followUp: What happens to an enzyme's activity when the temperature rises above its optimum temperature?

rubric.why: Describes the effect of rising temperature up to the optimum.
rubric.description: The rate of enzyme action increases as temperature rises up to the enzyme's optimum temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate rises up to an optimum temperature.

rubric.why: Explains why high temperatures reduce enzyme activity.
rubric.description: Above the optimum, the enzyme may denature, changing its active site and decreasing the reaction rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking denaturation or a changed active site with a fall in rate.

modelAnswer: As temperature rises, the rate of enzyme action increases up to the enzyme's optimum temperature.
Above the optimum, the enzyme may denature; its active site changes shape and the rate of enzyme action decreases.

items.followUp: Explain the tissue and organ-system levels of organization, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of an organ and a suitable example.
rubric.description: An organ is made of different tissues working together to perform a specific function; for example, the stomach.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition and 1 mark for a suitable example.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of an organ system and a suitable example.
rubric.description: An organ system is a group of organs working together to perform a major function; for example, the digestive system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition and 1 mark for a suitable example.

modelAnswer: An organ is made up of different tissues that work together to perform a specific function; for example, the stomach.
An organ system is a group of organs that work together to perform a major function; for example, the digestive system.
